learn.intro: Jev answers typed questions: a Choice, a Noul, a Score. It has no way to write text. Here both racers get the same job: write a 4-line poem about a topic.

compare.title: Jev, a System One model
points: Returns typed answers as data, not sentences
Has no question type for free text
Is built to judge, not to write

compare.title: An LLM, a System Two model
points: Writes free text, so a poem is ordinary work
Charges for every token it writes
Takes longer, because it writes word by word

predict.intro: On the Play step, Jev and an LLM each get the same job: write a 4-line poem for each of 3 topics. Guess who hands in a finished poem for every topic.

questions.prompt: Who writes a finished poem for every topic?

why: Jev answers with typed data, and none of its question types holds a poem. Asked for one anyway, the real API response is shown above: that is what it sends back, not something we wrote.
The LLM writes free text, so it can answer any topic. That is System Two work: slower and billed per token written, but open-ended.
Use Jev to judge or sort what a model has written, and an LLM to write it.

questions.prompt: You need a friendly 4-line message written for each new customer. Which tool fits?

options.text: Jev: it returns typed answers quickly
An LLM: it writes free text
Plain code: a template can never sound natural

questions.explanation: Writing is open-ended text, which is System Two work. Jev only returns typed answers. A template is fine for fixed wording, but not for a message that has to read as new each time.

questions.prompt: Why could Jev not write the poem?

options.text: Its answers are typed data (a Choice, Noul or Score), with no question type for free text
It was too slow to finish in time
The topics were too hard for it

questions.explanation: Jev reads and judges, then returns data. The API has no question type that holds a poem, so the request is refused, whatever the topic.
